quote: (i) The Servicer will indemnify the Issuer, the Owner Trustee and the Indenture Trustee (including in its capacity as Note Paying Agent), and their officers, directors, employees and agents (each, an "Indemnified Person") for all fees, expenses, losses, claims, actions, suits, damages and liabilities (including reasonable legal fees and expenses) resulting from the Servicer's (including in its capacity as Custodian) willful misconduct, bad faith or gross negligence in performing its obligations under the Transaction Documents
rationale: Section 6.3 contains a counterparty-side indemnity running in our favour: Cellco as Servicer (and separately as Marketing Agent) indemnifies the Issuer, Owner Trustee and Indenture Trustee and their personnel for all fees, expenses, losses, claims, damages and liabilities (including reasonable legal fees) resulting from its willful misconduct, bad faith or gross negligence, including costs of enforcing the indemnity. Section 6.3(b) supplies standard procedure (prompt notice that is not a condition unless prejudicial, Servicer/Marketing Agent may assume defence with counsel reasonably satisfactory to us, separate counsel at its cost on conflict, no settlement implying our acknowledgement without consent), and Section 6.3(c) provides survival past resignation, termination and trust termination. The indemnity is uncapped (no super-cap or fee-based ceiling) and there is no reciprocal Issuer/Depositor indemnity of the Servicer anywhere in the Agreement, so we sit at or above the preferred position on the material terms (Vendor indemnity for gross negligence/wilful misconduct plus standard procedure, with our own indemnity narrower than "narrow"). Section 7.5(c) additionally puts servicing-transition expenses on the resigning or terminated Servicer. Sub-elements short of preferred, noted only: there is no IP-infringement indemnity (atypical and commercially inapposite for a receivables securitisation with no services/deliverables licensed to us), no express standalone trigger for breach of applicable law or unauthorised disclosure of data (though Section 6.2(a) preserves liability for the Servicer's own willful misconduct, bad faith or gross negligence, and Exhibit A privacy/data protection policies apply), and the Depositor is not itself named as an Indemnified Person. These are not material failures of the fallback, so no redline.

quote: On and after the Closing Date or Acquisition Date, as applicable, until a Receivable has been paid in full, acquired or sold to a third party under Section 3.4, the Servicer will mark its receivables systems to indicate clearly that the Receivable is owned by the Issuer and has been pledged to the Indenture Trustee under the Indenture.
rationale: Direction of ownership runs in our favour throughout. Section 2.1(a)/(b) has the Depositor "transfer and absolutely assign to the Issuer... all of the Depositor's right, title and interest" in the Receivables and related Depositor Transferred Property; Section 9.2 bars any further transfer or Lien; Section 9.4(a) requires Cellco to flag its own receivables systems to show the Receivables are owned by the Issuer; and Section 3.10(b) has the Custodian hold the Receivable Files "for the benefit of the Issuer and the Indenture Trustee", with Section 7.5(b) requiring delivery of the Receivable Files and the accounts and records to a Successor Servicer. Nothing assigns our property, records or obligor data to Cellco, and no joint ownership is created, so there is no walk-away exposure. This is a securitisation transfer and servicing agreement rather than a procurement contract, so there is no classic deliverables/work-product IP clause; the only counterparty-favourable carve-out is Section 7.5(b), under which the Servicer "will not be obligated to provide, license or assign its processes, procedures, models, servicing software or other applications" — that is Cellco retaining its own platform, tools and know-how, which the playbook expressly permits and which sits at the fallback position (vendor keeps generic tools; we keep the files, records and data we own). We note in passing the absence of an express licence-back of servicing software or systems to support a servicing transition, which is a sub-element short of the preferred position but not a material failure warranting a redline here.

quote: (a) Liability for Specific Obligations. Each of the Servicer and the Marketing Agent, severally and not jointly, will be liable under this Agreement only for its specific obligations under this Agreement. All other liability is expressly waived and released as a condition of, and consideration for, the execution of this Agreement by the Servicer or the Marketing Agent, as applicable. Each of the Servicer and the Marketing Agent, severally and not jointly, will be liable only for its own willful misconduct, bad faith or gross negligence in performing its obligations under this Agreement.
rationale:
The liability architecture here is mutual and, on its material terms, sits at or above the fallback, so no redline is warranted.

1. Mutuality: Section 6.2(a) (p0283) limits the Servicer's and Marketing Agent's liability to their specific obligations and to their own willful misconduct, bad faith or gross negligence. Section 5.2(a) (p0243) applies word-for-word the same limitation to the Depositor. The limitation is therefore symmetrical and not a one-sided vendor shield — the walk-away scenario (our liability uncapped while the counterparty's is capped) does not arise.

2. No monetary cap on the counterparty: there is no dollar or months-of-fees cap anywhere in the Agreement (no "aggregate liability", "shall not exceed" or consequential-damages exclusion language; the only damages limitation found is the arbitral panel's limited remedial power at p0469). For us this is better than the preferred 12-months'-fees / USD 1,000,000 formulation. Importing a fees-based cap would be actively adverse: the Servicing Fee in this structure is a small monthly percentage of principal balance, so a 12-month-fees cap would be illusory and would materially reduce Cellco's exposure. Consistent with the rule's own warning about caps measured against a small fee base, we should not propose one.

3. Carve-outs: the Servicer's and Marketing Agent's indemnities under Section 6.3(a) (p0291, p0292) run to the Issuer, Owner Trustee and Indenture Trustee for all fees, expenses, losses, claims, damages and liabilities resulting from willful misconduct, bad faith or gross negligence, with no cap and no super-cap ceiling. Indemnification, gross negligence and willful misconduct — the fallback's minimum carve-out set — are all outside any limitation, and "bad faith" substantially covers the fraud carve-out.

4. Our side is additionally protected: Section 9.6 (p0378) limits any claim against the Depositor or the Issuer to the Depositor Transferred Property, an effective ceiling on our exposure that the counterparty does not enjoy.

Noted but not flagged (minor sub-elements per the classification rules): there is no express uncapped carve-out for confidentiality, data protection/security or infringement of our IP, no separate fraud carve-out beyond "bad faith", and no mutual indirect/consequential damages exclusion. Given that the counterparty carries no monetary cap at all and its indemnities are uncapped, these omissions do not defeat the fallback and are recorded for information rather than redlined. This is a securitization transfer and servicing agreement rather than a commercial supply contract, and the exculpation-plus-uncapped-indemnity model is the market-standard equivalent of the playbook position.

quote: (a) Assignment. Except as stated in Sections 5.3, 7.4 and 7.6, this Agreement may not be assigned by the Depositor or the Servicer without the consent of the Owner Trustee, the Indenture Trustee, the Certificateholders and the Noteholders of at least 66-2/3% of the Note Balance of the Controlling Class.
rationale: The assignment architecture is symmetric and preserves our successor rights, so it sits at or above the fallback. Section 10.2(a) is expressly subject to Sections 5.3, 7.4 and 7.6: Section 5.3 lets our Depositor pass this Agreement to any Person into which it merges or consolidates, that succeeds to its business, or that is an Affiliate to whom it assigns, without counterparty consent — the affiliate/successor and M&A carve-out the preferred position requires (the 15-Business-Day assumption agreement, Officer's Certificate/Opinion and Rating Agency notice are mechanical successor formalities, close to the fallback's "written notice"). Section 7.6 gives Cellco as Servicer the mirror-image right, and the residual consent gate in 10.2(a) runs to the Owner Trustee, Indenture Trustee and Noteholders (investor protection) rather than to Cellco, so the counterparty holds no veto over our assignments. The Issuer's ability to assign and pledge to the Indenture Trustee is expressly acknowledged (Section 2.2), and Section 10.2(b) binds permitted successors and assigns. On change of control: the phrase appears nowhere in the Agreement, and there is no Cellco right to terminate, re-price or refuse consent on a change of control of the Issuer or Depositor — to the contrary, Section 7.1 bars Cellco from resigning as Servicer unless it is legally unable to perform. The Class A Certificateholder's Optional Acquisition/Optional Redemption rights (Sections 8.1–8.2) are principal-balance and date triggered, not change-of-control triggered, so they are not a walk-away exit right. Noted but not flagged: consent under 10.2(a) is not qualified by a "not unreasonably withheld" standard and there is no express bar on assignment to a competitor, both minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording in a structured-finance deal where the consent parties are the trustees and noteholders.

No change-of-control trigger exists: the phrase does not appear and no Vendor/Servicer termination, re-pricing or consent right keys off a change of control; Section 7.1 in fact bars the Servicer from resigning absent legal inability, so walk-away territory is avoided. proposal.comment: [Playbook] We need a licence of the servicing processes, models and software so that a Successor Servicer (or our Affiliates and contractors) can actually service the Receivables on a servicing transfer; as drafted the Servicer may simply refuse, which leaves us with no path to continuity. We have therefore added a non-exclusive, irrevocable, royalty-free licence extending to our Affiliates and contractors and transferable to successors, while preserving the carve-outs for genuine third-party transfer restrictions and legal, regulatory, privacy and data protection limits.

ops.newText: The Servicer hereby grants to the Issuer, its Affiliates and its contractors acting on its behalf (including any Successor Servicer) a non-exclusive, irrevocable, royalty-free license, transferable to any successor to the Issuer and to any Successor Servicer, to use the Servicer's processes, procedures, models, servicing software and other applications solely to the extent necessary to service the Receivables, and the Servicer will provide, license or assign the same to any Successor Servicer on request; provided, that the Servicer will not be obligated to provide anything covered by a restriction on transfer or assignment in favor of an unaffiliated third party or a confidentiality agreement with an unaffiliated third party, or otherwise restricted by legal, regulatory, privacy or data protection policies.

proposal.summary: Replace the Servicer's blanket refusal to license servicing systems with an irrevocable, transferable licence to the Issuer, its Affiliates and its contractors (including any Successor Servicer), retaining the legal/regulatory and third-party restriction carve-outs.

quote: The Servicer will not be obligated to provide, license or assign its processes, procedures, models, servicing software or other applications to any Successor Servicer or any third party, or provide anything covered by a restriction on transfer or assignment or a confidentiality agreement or otherwise restricted by legal, regulatory, privacy or data protection policies.
rationale: Section 7.5(b) is the only provision in the Agreement that addresses licensing of the Servicer's systems, and it lands squarely in walk-away territory: the Servicer is expressly not obligated to provide, license or assign its processes, models or servicing software to any Successor Servicer or third party, so there is no licence at all to the Issuer, its Affiliates or the contractors/Successor Servicer who would need to run the servicing platform, and no path to add them. That fails both the preferred position (licence extending to affiliates and contractors, irrevocable, transferable to successors) and the fallback (affiliates covered on notice, transferable to a successor). The restriction operates against us (Issuer/Depositor) on a servicing transfer, so it is properly flagged. Our redline converts the carve-out into a non-exclusive, irrevocable, royalty-free licence to the Issuer, its Affiliates and its contractors including any Successor Servicer, transferable to successors and limited to what is necessary to service the Receivables, while preserving the Servicer's legitimate carve-outs for genuine third-party transfer/confidentiality restrictions and legal, regulatory, privacy and data protection limits.

quote: Section 3.6 Review of Servicer's Records. The Servicer will maintain records and documents relating to its performance under this Agreement according to its customary business practices. Upon reasonable request not more than once during any calendar year, and with reasonable notice, the Servicer will give the Issuer, the Depositor, the Parent Support Provider, the Administrator, the Owner Trustee and the Indenture Trustee (or their representatives) access to the records and documents to conduct a review of the Servicer's performance under this Agreement.
rationale: No audit, inspection or verification right binds our party. Every review/access right in the Agreement runs against the counterparty (Cellco as Servicer and as Custodian) and in favour of the Issuer/Depositor: Section 3.6 (p0131) gives us access to the Servicer's records, capped at once per calendar year on reasonable notice, at the Servicer's offices during normal business hours; Section 3.4(e) (p0146) gives the Depositor and Issuer access to the Receivable Files and receivables systems; Article XIV (p0444-p0446) requires the Servicer to grant the Asset Representations Reviewer access to Review Materials; and p0437 plus the Form of Annual Certification (p1045-p1052) impose the Regulation AB Compliance Statement, Servicing Assessment, Attestation Report and annual certification on the Servicer as deliverables to us. The term "audit" does not appear in the document, and targeted searches surfaced no reciprocal right for Cellco in any capacity to inspect the Issuer's or Depositor's records, no unannounced or unlimited review right against us, and no remote access to our systems (the one Custodian-to-Servicer access provision at p0146 is internal to the counterparty's own roles). The rule's protective purpose is therefore satisfied in full at the preferred level, since there is no audit exposure to constrain; this is not a "missing" finding because the rule exists only to cap audits of our party, not to create a right in our favour. Noted for completeness rather than as a deviation: the reviews we do hold under Section 3.6 and 3.4(e) are silent on cost allocation and are subject to the Servicer's confidentiality, privacy and data protection policies, but these are rights benefiting us and are outside the scope of this rule.

quote: Section 10.6 Submission to Jurisdiction. Each party submits to the nonexclusive jurisdiction of the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York and of any New York State Court sitting in New York, New York for legal proceedings relating to this Agreement.
rationale: Section 10.5 elects the internal laws of the State of New York (including GOL §§ 5-1401/5-1402) and even bars any amendment changing the governing law away from New York, which matches our preferred position. Section 10.6 submits the parties to the jurisdiction of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York and the New York State courts sitting in New York, New York, with waiver of venue and forum non conveniens objections — the preferred New York County forum. The Article XI dispute resolution provisions do not displace the courts: mediation or binding arbitration is available only at the Requesting Party's election in respect of reacquisition requests (Section 11.2(a) expressly preserves the option to "institute a legal proceeding"), any such proceeding is held in New York, New York (Section 11.2(d)(i)), the neutrals must be experienced in New York law, and awards are enforceable in any court of competent jurisdiction. There is no mandatory arbitration and no foreign seat, so no walk-away risk. The only departure from the preferred wording is that the submission to jurisdiction is nonexclusive rather than exclusive; that is a minor sub-element (and preserves our own flexibility to sue elsewhere), so we note it rather than redline it.

No mandatory or foreign-seated arbitration: Article XI mediation/arbitration is elective for the Requesting Party (Section 11.2(a) preserves the right to institute a legal proceeding) and any such proceeding is seated in New York, New York (Section 11.2(d)(i)), so there is no walk-away exposure. quote: Section 9.3 Expenses. The Depositor will pay the expenses to perform its obligations under this Agreement and the Issuer's and the Indenture Trustee's reasonable expenses to perfect the Issuer's interest in the Depositor Transferred Property and to enforce the Depositor's obligations under this Agreement.
rationale: This is a securitization transfer and servicing agreement with no pricing or most-favoured-nation construct anywhere. Searches for "most favored", "no less favorable", "favorable", "pricing" and "terms and conditions offered to" returned no MFN language, and a full read of Article IX (Other Agreements) confirms it contains only perfection, expense, no-petition, limited-recourse, tax and cap-collateral provisions. Neither the Issuer nor the Depositor is obliged to extend to Cellco (as Servicer/Marketing Agent/Originator) terms no less favourable than those given to third parties, or to match third-party offers. This meets the preferred position — no MFN obligation burdening our party — so no redline is required.

quote: (i) From time to time, the Class A Certificateholder may, solely at its option, deposit amounts into the Acquisition Account, as set forth in Section 2.5 of the Trust Agreement.
rationale: No minimum purchase commitment, take-or-pay or volume restriction is imposed on our side. The only recurring "purchase" mechanic is the acquisition of Additional Receivables in Article II, and it is entirely discretionary and condition-based: funding of the Acquisition Account is made by the Class A Certificateholder "solely at its option" (p0223), and each transfer is "[s]ubject to the satisfaction of the conditions in Section 2.1(d)" — a Transfer Notice plus satisfaction of the Credit Enhancement Test and Pool Composition Tests (p0037, p0039). The Issuer pays only the Additional Receivables Cash Transfer Amount actually withdrawn from the Acquisition Account for receivables it acquires (p0224), excess amounts are released to Certificateholders (p0225), and the account is swept on entry into the Amortization Period (p0226), which operates as the exit. The Required Acquisition Deposit and Required Negative Carry Amount are structural funding mechanics tied to amounts the Certificateholder chose to deposit, not a shortfall penalty. The only "shortfall" obligation found (p0211) runs against the Marketing Agent in our favour. This meets the preferred position (fees/consideration for assets actually acquired, no committed volume), so no redline.

quote: Section 9.2 No Transfer or Lien by Depositor. Except for the transfer and assignment under this Agreement, the Depositor will not transfer or assign any Depositor Transferred Property to another Person or Grant or allow a Lien, other than a Permitted Lien, on an interest in any Depositor Transferred Property.
rationale: This transfer and servicing agreement contains no employee non-solicitation, no-hire or inducement covenant. Searches for "solicit", "hire", "induce" and "personnel" returned no hits, and the only "employee" references are limited-recourse/no-recourse-against-personnel provisions (p0244, p0284), indemnity definitions (p0291) and ERISA/Benefit Plan definitions (p0649, p0651, p0740, p0770) — none of which restrict hiring. Article IX ("Other Agreements") contains only financing statement, no-transfer/lien, expense, no-petition, limited recourse, tax and cap collateral covenants, with no restrictive covenants on personnel; Article VII's successor servicer transition provisions likewise impose no hiring restriction on the Issuer, Depositor or any Successor Servicer. Because the playbook's preferred position is that no non-solicit bind the Customer, the absence of any such covenant meets the preferred position and no redline is warranted.

quote: Section 8.3 Termination. This Agreement will terminate on the earlier to occur of (a) the date upon which the last remaining Receivable is paid in full, settled, sold or written off and any amounts received are applied and (b) the Issuer is terminated under Section 8.1 of the Trust Agreement.
rationale: Searches for "renew", "renewal", "automatically renew", "initial term" and "extended term" return no hits, and Article VIII (Termination) contains only the Optional Acquisition/Clean-Up Redemption (8.1), Optional Redemption (8.2) and a self-executing termination provision (8.3). The Agreement's term runs to the earlier of payment/settlement of the last Receivable or termination of the Issuer under the Trust Agreement — there is no automatic renewal term, no non-renewal notice window and no renewal price-uplift mechanic, so none of the evergreen or uplift risks the rule targets arise. Servicer resignation/termination and successor servicer mechanics in Article VII give the Issuer exit rights independent of any renewal cycle. This is at least as protective as the preferred position (no renewal absent mutual agreement), so no redline is warranted; inserting an opt-out/CPI-cap construct into a securitization transfer and servicing agreement would be structurally inapposite.

verification.notes: Claimed status is compliant and no redline or comment is proposed, which is the expected output for a compliant finding — nothing over-flagged. Absence of auto-renewal is at least as protective as the preferred position (renewal only by mutual written agreement); classifying as compliant rather than 'missing' is correct because the rule's risk (hard-to-exit evergreen terms) cannot materialize here. proposal.comment: [Playbook] Article VII lets us remove Cellco only on a Servicer Termination Event (and then only through the Indenture Trustee), so we have no ability to exit this multi-year servicing engagement without cause. We have added a 30 days' notice termination-for-convenience right in our favour, with no termination fee and a refund of Servicing Fees prepaid for the post-termination period, dovetailed into the existing Successor Servicer machinery in Sections 7.3 through 7.5. If 30 days is too tight operationally, we can live with 60-90 days' notice.

ops.text: Section 7.1A Termination for Convenience by the Issuer. In addition to any other right of removal or termination under this Agreement, the Issuer, at the direction of the Depositor, may terminate the rights and obligations of the Servicer under this Agreement for convenience, in whole or in part, at any time upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to the Servicer, the Owner Trustee and the Indenture Trustee, without payment by the Issuer or the Depositor of any termination fee, penalty, make-whole or other compensation, and the Servicer will refund any Servicing Fee paid in respect of the period after the effective date of such termination. Sections 7.3, 7.4 and 7.5 will apply to a termination under this Section 7.1A as if the Servicer had been terminated under Section 7.2(c).

proposal.summary: Add an Issuer right to terminate the Servicer for convenience on 30 days' notice, without penalty and with refund of prepaid Servicing Fees.

quote: Section 7.1 No Resignation. The Servicer will not resign as Servicer under this Agreement unless it determines it is legally unable to perform its obligations under this Agreement.
rationale: The Vendor side of this rule is satisfied and then some: Section 7.1 bars Cellco from resigning as Servicer except where it is legally unable to perform, and Section 7.3 requires it to keep performing until a Successor Servicer accepts engagement — better than the preferred position (no Vendor convenience right during the term). The customer side fails, however. Our only exit from the servicing engagement is Section 7.2, which requires a Servicer Termination Event (payment failure, material breach uncured for 90 days, or Insolvency Event) and vests the removal right in the Indenture Trustee at the direction of the Controlling Class, not in the Issuer or the Depositor; Section 8.3 otherwise runs the Agreement until the last Receivable is paid in full, settled, sold or written off. There is no termination-for-convenience right for us anywhere in the document (a full-text search for "convenience" returns only the headings clause at Section 10.10), and the term plainly exceeds 12 months. Under the detection guidance that absence is a deviation (missing behaviour) rather than a missing clause, since a usable termination architecture (Articles VII and VIII) does exist. Redline proposed (ok:true): a new Section 7.1A giving the Issuer, at the Depositor's direction, a 30 days' notice convenience termination right with no fee or penalty and a refund of prepaid Servicing Fees, plugged into the existing Sections 7.3–7.5 transition machinery so noteholder continuity is preserved; the fallback of 60–90 days' notice is offered in the comment. Noted but not separately flagged: the Optional Acquisition (Section 8.1) and Optional Redemption (Section 8.2) exits sit with the Class A Certificateholder, defined at p0668 as "the Originators or their designee" (i.e., the counterparty side), and are exercisable on only ten (10) days' notice. That is not a Vendor walk-away from service in the playbook sense — it requires the pool price to be "as agreed upon by the Class A Certificateholder and the Issuer" and requires the Notes, accrued interest, Make-Whole Payments and all other Issuer obligations to be paid in full — so we have not double-flagged the notice period.
sectionRef: § VII SERVICER RESIGNATION AND TERMINATION; SUCCESSOR SERVICER

verification.notes: Classification is defensible: Article VII gives the Issuer no cause-free exit (removal only on a Servicer Termination Event, and then exercisable by the Indenture Trustee at the Controlling Class's direction), and Section 8.3 runs the Agreement until the last Receivable is paid, so the engagement plainly exceeds 12 months with no customer convenience right — exactly the 'missing behaviour' deviation contemplated by the detection guidance. Vendor side correctly assessed as better than preferred (Section 7.1 no-resignation plus Section 7.3 continued performance until a Successor Servicer accepts), and the drafter did not over-flag it; the Section 8.1/8.2 Optional Acquisition/Redemption 10-day notice is reasonably explained as not a servicer walk-away, avoiding a double flag. Redline is minimal and additive: a single new Section 7.1A granting a 30 days' notice convenience termination with no fee/penalty and a refund of prepaid Servicing Fees, expressly routed through the existing Sections 7.3–7.5 successor machinery so no existing operative text is disturbed. It tracks the model language and the preferred position. The failed deterministic check ('Customer convenience termination present') is a phrasing variant only — the right is conferred on the Issuer/Depositor, which are our-side parties in this document, and the inserted text plainly grants for-convenience termination on 30 days' notice. Comment is accurate, concise, in the required voice, explains the change and cites the fallback (60–90 days' notice) without lecturing. Caveat (non-fatal): in this ABS structure the Issuer is an SPE and the Depositor a Verizon affiliate, and removal rights are deliberately vested in the Indenture Trustee for noteholder protection, so the practical leverage of this ask is limited and counterparty/rating-agency pushback should be expected; severity is better treated as medium.

quote: (a) Cooperation on Termination. On its resignation or termination, the Servicer will cooperate with the Issuer, the Owner Trustee, the Indenture Trustee and the Successor Servicer in effecting (i) the termination of its rights and obligations under this Agreement and (ii) an orderly transition of such rights and obligations to the Successor Servicer.
rationale: Section 7.5 is a full transition-assistance and records-return clause running in our favour: the outgoing Servicer (Cellco) must cooperate in an orderly transition, and "[a]s soon as practicable after the effective date of its resignation or termination" must transfer all funds relating to the Receivables and "deliver to the Successor Servicer the Receivable Files and the accounts and records maintained by the Servicer" (p0344/p0346). Section 7.3 requires the Servicer to keep performing until a Successor Servicer accepts its engagement (or the stated termination date), which is an open-ended assistance period exceeding the preferred six months, and Section 7.5(c) puts all reasonable transition expenses on the resigning or terminated Servicer rather than on us at its then-current rates — both better than the playbook preferred position. There is no immediate-deletion or no-return risk (walk-away). Minor sub-elements short of the preferred wording are noted only: delivery is "as soon as practicable" rather than a fixed 30 days, no machine-readable format is specified, and there is no post-transition deletion certification; Section 7.5(b) also carves out the Servicer's proprietary processes, models and software and items restricted by confidentiality or data-protection rules. These are proportionate in a securitization servicing transfer (and Section 3.12(b)/Exhibit A require continued cooperation and data-protection compliance), so we do not redline.
ruleTitle: Post-termination transition assistance and data return
sectionRef: § VII SERVICER RESIGNATION AND TERMINATION; SUCCESSOR SERVICER

verification.notes: Cited Section 7.5 is a genuine post-termination transition and records-return clause: cooperation in an orderly transition (7.5(a)), transfer of funds and delivery of Receivable Files and servicing records to the Successor Servicer (7.5(b)), and transition expenses borne by the outgoing Servicer (7.5(c)), with Section 7.3 requiring continued performance until a Successor Servicer accepts engagement — meeting or exceeding the fallback (and in expense allocation, the preferred) position. No walk-away trigger is present: there is no immediate deletion of, or refusal to return, our data/records. Shortfalls versus preferred wording ('as soon as practicable' rather than 30 days, no machine-readable format specification, no deletion certification, and the proprietary-software/confidentiality carve-out) are correctly treated as minor sub-elements noted in the rationale rather than redlined, consistent with the classification semantics. Consistent with a compliant finding, no redline or counterparty comment was proposed; the rendered text is unchanged from the original paragraphs. The failed deterministic keyword check is a phrasing artifact (the clause uses securitization vocabulary — 'Transition of Servicing', 'Receivable Files', 'accounts and records' — rather than 'data export/return'), not evidence of a missing clause.

ops.text: Section 10.14 Insurance. Each of the Servicer and the Marketing Agent will maintain, at its own expense, throughout the term of this Agreement and for one (1) year thereafter: (a) commercial general liability insurance of not less than $1,000,000 per occurrence and $2,000,000 in the aggregate; (b) professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance of not less than $2,000,000; (c) for so long as it holds, processes or has access to Personally Identifiable Information of Obligors, cyber liability insurance of not less than $5,000,000; and (d) workers' compensation insurance as required by applicable Law. Each of the Servicer and the Marketing Agent will deliver certificates of insurance evidencing such coverage to the Issuer, the Depositor and the Indenture Trustee on request.

Searches for "insurance", "fidelity bond" and "errors and omissions" return only unrelated references (billed insurance premiums in the Servicing Procedures at p0095 and FDIC deposit insurance at p0903); Article VI (Servicer and Marketing Agent) contains representations, liability, indemnity and delegation provisions but no coverage requirement, and Article X Miscellaneous runs through Section 10.13 with no insurance section. This matters because Cellco, as Servicer/Custodian, holds and processes Obligor Personally Identifiable Information (see p0446) and may contract with other Persons to perform its obligations (Section 6.4, p0300), so the playbook's walk-away scenario (no insurance for a vendor processing personal data) is engaged. The Servicer's indemnity at Section 6.3 is limited to willful misconduct, bad faith or gross negligence and does not substitute for insurance. Proposed new Section 10.14 at the preferred position (CGL USD 1M/2M, E&O USD 2M, cyber USD 5M, workers' compensation, certificates on request), with the fallback (E&O USD 1M / cyber USD 2M) offered in the comment.
